lessons.title: Frogs, Hens and Cows: Many Ways to One Goal – How Do Animals Reproduce?

quiz.prompt: Near Kisumu, a learner looks at frogspawn in a pond and a hen's egg in a nest. Which statement correctly describes what is seen?
choices: Both frog eggs and hen's eggs are hard-shelled and laid on land.
Frog eggs are covered in jelly and released into water, while a hen's egg is hard-shelled and laid on land.
Frog eggs are hard-shelled and laid on land, while a hen's egg is covered in jelly and released into water.
Both frog eggs and hen's eggs are covered in jelly and released into water.
quiz.rationale: The images show jelly-covered frog eggs released into pond water and a hen's hard-shelled egg laid on land. This is only a description of what is seen, not an explanation.
quiz.placement: Predict: viewing the photos of frogspawn in a Kisumu wetland pond and a hen on eggs

quiz.prompt: A learner claims that 'all animals lay eggs'. Which animal from the lesson photos does NOT fit this claim?
choices: A frog in a pond near Kisumu
A cow with her calf
A tilapia in Lake Victoria
A hen sitting on her eggs
quiz.rationale: A cow gives birth to a live calf after months of development inside her body, so the claim 'all animals lay eggs' does not fit. Frogs, hens and tilapia all produce eggs.
quiz.placement: Predict: teacher checklist for misconceptions such as 'all animals lay eggs'

quiz.prompt: Which statement matches what is described about the number of young in the anchoring phenomenon?
choices: A frog gives birth to a few live young, while a cow lays one hard-shelled egg.
A cow lays thousands of eggs, while a frog gives birth to one live calf.
A frog releases thousands of eggs into water, while a cow gives birth to one live calf after months of development inside her.
A frog and a cow both produce thousands of young at one time.
quiz.rationale: Frogs release thousands of jelly-covered eggs, while a cow has one calf after months of internal development. At this stage learners only record this pattern, and why it happens is still an open question.
quiz.placement: Predict: prediction 'Why do frogs need thousands of eggs but a cow produces one calf?'

quiz.prompt: Your group is going to observe frogspawn at the edge of a school pond. Which rule is correct?
choices: Collect the spawn in your pockets so you can study it in class.
Wade into the pond and pick up the spawn to count the eggs.
Touch the spawn with bare hands, but only for a short time.
Observe from the edge, do not touch the spawn with bare hands, and wash your hands afterwards.
quiz.rationale: The lesson rules are to observe from the edge, not to touch spawn with bare hands, and to wash hands afterwards.
quiz.placement: Part A: observing external fertilisation at the school pond or wetland edge

quiz.prompt: A group is filling in its Part A observation table for frog spawn. Which entry is an observation, not an explanation?
choices: Water helps the sperm to reach the eggs.
The eggs are released into the water and are surrounded by a jelly layer.
The jelly stops the eggs from drying out.
Frogs need thousands of eggs because many are eaten.
quiz.rationale: Saying where the eggs are and what surrounds them is a direct observation. The other entries claim reasons for what is seen, and the table is for recording what is seen.
quiz.placement: Part A: recording where eggs are released, jelly coating and number of eggs in the observation table

quiz.prompt: In Part B, a group sorts a hen and a cow on the classification chart. Which placement is correct?
choices: Hen: ovoviviparous; cow: oviparous
Hen: oviparous (eggs laid, development outside the body); cow: viviparous (young develop inside the mother and are born live)
Hen: viviparous; cow: ovoviviparous
Hen: viviparous; cow: oviparous
quiz.rationale: A hen lays eggs that develop outside her body, so it is oviparous. A cow carries the young inside her and gives birth to a live calf, so it is viviparous.
quiz.placement: Part B: sorting animals into oviparous, viviparous and ovoviviparous columns on the classification chart

quiz.prompt: A source says that in a female guppy the eggs develop and hatch inside her body, and she does not feed them through a placenta-type connection. In which column should the group place the guppy?
choices: Ovoviviparous, because eggs develop and hatch inside her body without placenta-type feeding
Oviparous, because the eggs hatch
Viviparous, because the young develop inside her
Oviparous, because it produces eggs
quiz.rationale: Ovoviviparous animals keep the eggs inside the body where they develop and hatch, without placenta-type nourishment from the mother. This matches the guppy description.
quiz.placement: Part B: sorting shark/guppy into the ovoviviparous column on the classification chart

lessons.title: Built for Reproduction: Dissecting Mammalian Reproductive Structures

quiz.prompt: A Friesian cow in Kericho carries her calf for about nine months before birth. In which organ does the calf develop during this time?
choices: The uterus
The ovary
The oviduct
The stomach
quiz.rationale: The uterus has a thick muscular wall and a rich lining that supports the embryo as it grows. The stomach is part of the digestive system, not the reproductive system. The oviduct carries the egg, and the ovary makes eggs.
quiz.placement: Predict: sketch of what is inside a female and male mammal (Friesian cow and frog pond images)

quiz.prompt: In a male rat, the testes hang outside the main body cavity. What is the main advantage of this position?
choices: It stores the embryo safely until birth
It lets urine and sperm leave through separate tubes
It keeps the sperm cooler than the body temperature
It keeps the sperm warm so they develop faster
quiz.rationale: Sperm production works best at a temperature lower than normal body temperature, and the position of the testes outside the body provides this.
quiz.placement: Part A: dissection of a small mammal (male specimen groups locating the testes and epididymis)

quiz.prompt: A group dissecting a male rabbit finds a long, tightly coiled tube lying against the testis. What is its function?
choices: It carries urine out of the body
It produces testosterone only
It is where fertilisation takes place
It stores sperm until they are released
quiz.rationale: This tube is the epididymis. Its coiled structure gives a long space to store sperm. Fertilisation happens in the female oviduct, and urine leaves through the urethra.
quiz.placement: Part A: dissection of a small mammal (male specimen: 'Where does the sperm duct meet the urethra?')

quiz.prompt: In a male mammal, the sperm duct joins another tube that leads through the penis. Which tube is this, and what does it carry?
choices: The epididymis, which carries urine only
The sperm duct, which carries urine only
The oviduct, which carries sperm only
The urethra, which carries both urine and sperm
quiz.rationale: The sperm duct joins the urethra. The urethra carries urine and sperm out of the body, though not at the same time. Some learners wrongly think urine and sperm use separate tubes all the way.
quiz.placement: Part A: dissection of a small mammal (male specimen: 'Where does the sperm duct meet the urethra?')

quiz.prompt: A female rabbit specimen has a pair of thin tubes lined with tiny hair-like cilia that lead from the ovaries to the uterus. What is the role of these tubes?
choices: They seal the uterus to protect the embryo
They move the egg along and are where fertilisation happens
They store the calf or pups until birth
They make the hormones FSH and LH
quiz.rationale: These are the oviducts. Their cilia move the egg towards the uterus, and fertilisation takes place in them. The cervix is the muscular seal, and FSH and LH come from the pituitary gland.
quiz.placement: Part A: dissection of a small mammal (female specimen groups locating the ovaries, oviducts, uterus and cervix)

quiz.prompt: Which feature of the uterus makes it well adapted to support a developing embryo?
choices: It has a thin wall so that the embryo can leave quickly
It makes the eggs that will be fertilised
It has a thick muscular wall and a rich lining where the embryo implants
It has cilia that carry the sperm to the egg
quiz.rationale: The rich lining allows the embryo to implant and receive support, and the muscular wall can stretch and protect the growing embryo. Eggs are made in the ovaries, and cilia are found in the oviducts.
quiz.placement: Structure-function table and Think-Pair-Share (explaining how one organ's structure helps it do its job)

quiz.prompt: A frog near Kisumu releases thousands of eggs into the pond, but a cow usually produces one calf at a time. Which statement best explains this difference?
choices: Cows have no ovaries, so they can only make one egg in a lifetime
A cow's embryo grows in the stomach, which only has room for one
Frogs have a uterus that can hold thousands of embryos
Frog eggs are fertilised outside the body and many are lost, while the cow's single embryo is protected and nourished inside the mother
quiz.rationale: External fertilisation exposes eggs to loss and predators, so frogs depend on large numbers. Mammals invest in protecting one embryo inside the uterus. Cows do have ovaries, and frogs do not develop embryos in a uterus.
quiz.placement: Structured debate: 'producing many gametes (frog) or protecting a single embryo inside the mother (cow/human)?'

quiz.prompt: A woman's oviducts are blocked, so the egg and sperm cannot meet. Which statement about how IVF can help is correct?
choices: Fertilisation can happen in a dish, and the early embryo is then placed in the uterus to develop
The embryo is placed in the stomach, where it grows
The baby grows wholly in a test tube until it is born
The sperm are made in the uterus instead of the testes
quiz.rationale: IVF bypasses the blocked oviduct by letting fertilisation happen outside the body. The embryo still develops in the mother's uterus. The belief that IVF babies grow wholly in a test tube is a common misconception.
quiz.placement: Revising the class 'Reproduction Strategies' model (note on where biotechnology like IVF could step in)

lessons.title: Built for the Journey: Structure of Sperm and Ovum

quiz.prompt: Before looking at any slides, a learner predicts that the human ovum will be much larger than a sperm cell. Which reason best supports this prediction?
choices: The ovum must be big enough to be seen by the sperm
The ovum has to swim a long distance, so it needs a big tail
The ovum has twice as many chromosomes as the sperm, so it takes up more space
The ovum stores food in its cytoplasm and has a protective layer, but it does not swim
quiz.rationale: The ovum does not move. It is large because it carries food reserves in its cytoplasm and has a protective layer (jelly coat/zona pellucida) to support the early embryo.
quiz.placement: Predict: sketching a sperm and an ovum and predicting which is bigger

quiz.prompt: Under a microscope, a learner sees that the midpiece of a sperm cell is packed with mitochondria. What is the function of this structure?
choices: It supplies the energy that the flagellum needs for swimming
It releases enzymes that digest the outer layer of the ovum
It protects the sperm from being damaged inside the female body
It stores the chromosomes that will be passed to the offspring
quiz.rationale: Mitochondria release energy by respiration. In the midpiece this energy powers the beating of the flagellum (tail) so the sperm can swim towards the ovum.
quiz.placement: Observe: drawing and labelling the sperm (midpiece with mitochondria)

quiz.prompt: A human sperm cell is about 50 micrometres long. A human ovum is about 0.1 mm across (1 mm = 1000 micrometres). About how many times wider is the ovum than the sperm is long?
choices: 5 times
200 times
20 times
2 times
quiz.rationale: Convert 0.1 mm to micrometres: 0.1 × 1000 = 100 micrometres. Then 100 ÷ 50 = 2, so the ovum is about 2 times the size of the sperm's length.
quiz.placement: Observe: observation table comparing size of sperm and ovum

quiz.prompt: During fertilisation, the acrosome at the head of the sperm releases enzymes. What do these enzymes do?
choices: They give the sperm energy to swim
They digest the jelly coat (zona pellucida) around the ovum so the sperm can enter
They make the ovum produce more food reserves
They join the sperm nucleus to the ovum nucleus
quiz.rationale: The acrosome contains digestive enzymes that break down the jelly coat/zona pellucida, allowing the sperm head to reach and fuse with the ovum. Energy for swimming comes from the mitochondria.
quiz.placement: Explain: CER frame on the functions of the acrosome, flagellum, mitochondria and jelly coat

quiz.prompt: Both the sperm and the ovum have haploid nuclei (half the normal number of chromosomes). Why is this important for fertilisation?
choices: Haploid nuclei let the ovum divide without a sperm
Haploid nuclei make the sperm lighter so it can swim faster
The fused nuclei give the zygote the full normal number of chromosomes
Haploid nuclei mean the offspring will have only half the genes of the mother
quiz.rationale: When the haploid sperm nucleus fuses with the haploid ovum nucleus, the zygote gets the full normal chromosome number. Without haploid gametes, the number would double in every generation.
quiz.placement: Explain: CER frame on the haploid nucleus of each gamete

quiz.prompt: A frog at the Lake Victoria wetlands releases thousands of eggs, but a cow usually gives birth to one calf. Which explanation best accounts for this difference?
choices: Cows cannot make more than one ovum because they have no jelly coat
Frogs have more sperm than cows, so they must also make more eggs
Frog eggs are fertilised in open water and have little protection, so many are lost, while a cow's fertilised egg is protected and nourished inside her body
Frog eggs are bigger than cow eggs, so more of them are needed
quiz.rationale: External fertilisation in water exposes frog eggs to predators and other dangers, so many eggs are needed for a few to survive. Internal fertilisation and development inside the cow protects the embryo, so one calf is enough.
quiz.placement: Explain: Think-Pair-Share on why frogs need thousands of eggs but cows only one calf

quiz.prompt: A news report says that in IVF the baby grows in a test tube from start to birth. Which statement correctly describes IVF?
choices: Fertilisation happens in a laboratory dish, and the embryo is then placed in the womb of the mother or a surrogate to develop
Fertilisation and the whole development of the baby happen in the laboratory
The ovum develops into a baby in the dish without any sperm
Fertilisation happens in the womb, and only the sperm is prepared in the laboratory
quiz.rationale: In IVF only fertilisation happens outside the body, in a dish. The embryo is then placed in the womb of the mother or a surrogate, where it grows until birth.
quiz.placement: Model: adding the arrow 'IVF: fertilisation in dish, embryo then placed in womb' to the class model

lessons.title: Hormonal Conductors: How Pituitary and Ovarian Hormones Regulate the Menstrual Cycle and Egg Release

quiz.prompt: On a normal 28-day menstrual cycle graph, a sudden sharp rise (surge) in one hormone around Day 14 is followed soon after by ovulation. Which hormone surge triggers the release of the egg from the ovary?
choices: Oestrogen
Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH)
Luteinising hormone (LH)
Progesterone
quiz.rationale: The LH surge around Day 14 triggers ovulation. FSH acts earlier to stimulate follicle growth, and progesterone rises only after ovulation.
quiz.placement: Observe: tracing FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone on the hormone charts and graph worksheets

quiz.prompt: After ovulation, the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum. Which hormone does the corpus luteum mainly release to keep the uterine lining thick and ready for a fertilised egg?
choices: Luteinising hormone (LH)
Progesterone
Oestrogen
Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH)
quiz.rationale: The corpus luteum mainly secretes progesterone, which maintains the thickened uterine lining in the second half of the cycle. Oestrogen's main role is the repair and thickening of the lining before ovulation.
quiz.placement: Observe: observation table (ovary event: corpus luteum; uterine lining: maintained/breakdown)

quiz.prompt: A woman's hormone graph shows normal FSH and oestrogen, but there is no LH surge in the middle of the cycle. What is the most likely effect?
choices: Ovulation takes place but progesterone rises too early
The egg is not released because ovulation does not take place
Several eggs are released at the same time
The uterine lining thickens twice in one cycle
quiz.rationale: The LH surge triggers ovulation, so without it the follicle does not release the egg. This is the 'absent LH surge, no ovulation' scenario, where fertility treatment may help.
quiz.placement: Observe: 'imbalance' scenario cards (absent LH surge with no ovulation)

quiz.prompt: In the second half of the cycle, oestrogen and progesterone levels are high. What do these high levels do to the pituitary gland, as an example of negative feedback?
choices: They make it release the egg directly
They stimulate it to release even more FSH and LH
They have no effect on it
They inhibit (reduce) the release of FSH and LH
quiz.rationale: High progesterone and oestrogen tell the pituitary to reduce FSH and LH, like a thermostat switching off heating. This stops new follicles developing while the lining is maintained.
quiz.placement: Explain: building the hormonal flowchart/concept map and labelling negative feedback arrows

quiz.prompt: Just before ovulation, oestrogen from the growing follicle reaches a high level. What does this high oestrogen do to LH release, as an example of positive feedback?
choices: It stops all LH release until menstruation
It triggers the LH surge
It causes menstruation to start
It turns the follicle into the uterine lining
quiz.rationale: High oestrogen switches from inhibiting LH to triggering the LH surge. This is positive feedback, and the surge then causes ovulation.
quiz.placement: Explain: building the hormonal flowchart/concept map and labelling positive feedback arrows

quiz.prompt: A woman at a clinic in Nairobi is given FSH injections as part of IVF treatment. Why is FSH given?
choices: To make the uterus grow a baby outside the body
To replace progesterone after ovulation
To stimulate several follicles to develop, so more than one egg can be collected
To stop menstruation permanently
quiz.rationale: FSH stimulates follicle growth. Injections make several follicles develop, whereas normally only one egg is released each cycle.
quiz.placement: Observe/DQB: link between imbalance scenario cards and why IVF patients receive FSH injections (DQB question 'How do IVF clinics in Nairobi use hormones?')

quiz.prompt: Many people believe IVF babies grow wholly in a test tube. Which statement is scientifically correct?
choices: IVF babies need no hormones at any stage of development
The baby grows in the test tube for nine months, then is placed in the mother
Only fertilisation happens in the laboratory; the baby develops in the mother's uterus
The baby develops in the ovary after fertilisation in the laboratory
quiz.rationale: In IVF, fertilisation takes place in the laboratory, and the embryo is then placed in the uterus, where development takes place. Hormones still play a role in preparing and maintaining the uterus.
quiz.placement: Model: adding the 'Hormonal control of gamete release' layer and correcting the IVF 'test tube baby' misconception

lessons.title: From Fertilisation to Birth: How Hormones and the Placenta Sustain Pregnancy

quiz.prompt: A cow carries one calf for about 9 months. How does the developing calf get its oxygen and food while inside the mother?
choices: The calf swallows food through its mouth and breathes air through its nose inside the uterus
The mother's blood flows directly into the calf's blood vessels and mixes with it
The calf uses only the yolk stored inside its body until birth
Substances diffuse across the thin membranes of the placenta between the mother's blood and the calf's blood
quiz.rationale: In mammals, the placenta lets oxygen and nutrients diffuse from mother to fetus across thin membranes, with no mixing of blood. Feeding by mouth, direct blood mixing and a yolk-only supply are the common misconceptions.
quiz.placement: Predict: sketch of how a baby inside a mother gets food and oxygen

quiz.prompt: Which statement about IVF babies is correct?
choices: The embryo is placed in the mother's uterus and still develops inside her body
The baby grows wholly in a test tube until birth
The baby grows inside the mother only for the first week and then in a machine
The baby does not need a placenta because it started in a laboratory
quiz.rationale: The lesson corrects the misconception that IVF babies grow in test tubes: embryos are placed in the uterus and develop with a placenta like any other pregnancy.
quiz.placement: Predict: recording misconceptions such as 'IVF babies grow in test tubes'

quiz.prompt: In humans, where does fertilisation normally take place, and where does the embryo then implant?
choices: Fertilisation in the oviduct; implantation in the uterine wall
Fertilisation in the vagina; implantation in the cervix
Fertilisation in the uterus; implantation in the oviduct
Fertilisation in the ovary; implantation in the placenta
quiz.rationale: The egg and sperm meet in the oviduct, and the embryo then embeds in the lining of the uterus (implantation). The placenta forms afterwards from this implantation.
quiz.placement: Observe: animation clips 1 and 2 (fertilisation in the oviduct, implantation and early hCG signalling)

quiz.prompt: A learner draws a placenta and marks where oxygen and nutrients pass from the mother to the baby. Which labelled part is the site where this exchange happens?
choices: The placenta, across thin membranes
The wall of the vagina
The amniotic fluid, where the baby absorbs food
The umbilical cord, where maternal blood mixes with fetal blood
quiz.rationale: Exchange occurs at the placenta by diffusion across thin membranes. The umbilical cord only carries fetal blood to and from the placenta, and the amniotic fluid protects the baby.
quiz.placement: Observe: drawing and labelling the placenta and umbilical cord, showing where exchange occurs

quiz.prompt: Why does the mother's blood not mix with the baby's blood in the placenta, even though substances pass between them?
choices: They have separate blood supplies, and substances move by diffusion across thin membranes
The umbilical cord pumps the mother's blood into the baby
The mother's red blood cells are too small to enter the baby's blood
Blood mixes only during labour, not during pregnancy
quiz.rationale: Maternal and fetal blood stay in separate vessels. Oxygen, nutrients and wastes diffuse across the thin placental membranes, so the blood itself never mixes.
quiz.placement: Explain: sentence frames 'The placenta allows ___ because ___' and addressing the misconception that blood mixes

quiz.prompt: After implantation, which hormone from the embryo keeps the corpus luteum active so that progesterone continues to maintain the uterine lining?
choices: Oestrogen in late pregnancy
Prolactin
Oxytocin
hCG
quiz.rationale: hCG signals the corpus luteum to stay active, so it keeps producing progesterone. Later the placenta takes over hormone production.
quiz.placement: Explain: building the hormonal flowchart (hCG keeps the corpus luteum active, progesterone maintains the lining)

quiz.prompt: At the end of pregnancy, oxytocin causes the uterus to contract. These contractions push the baby against the cervix, which causes more oxytocin to be released. What is this type of control called?
choices: Hormone mixing
Positive feedback
Negative feedback
Homeostasis
quiz.rationale: Each contraction leads to more oxytocin and stronger contractions, so the effect increases the cause. That is positive feedback, and it continues until birth.
quiz.placement: Explain: flowchart showing oxytocin triggering contractions (positive feedback)

quiz.prompt: A frog releases thousands of eggs in a pond, while a cow produces one calf at a time. Which statement best explains this difference?
choices: The cow's calf is protected and nourished inside the mother and cared for after birth, so fewer offspring are needed
Frog eggs have thick shells, so many are needed to break through them
The frog's eggs are fertilised inside the body, so many are needed
The cow has fewer eggs because cows are larger than frogs
quiz.rationale: Frogs use external fertilisation with little parental care, so many eggs are lost and many are needed. The cow's high parental investment means one well-supported calf is likely to survive.
quiz.placement: Model: comparison table of frog, hen and human/viviparous mammal (number of offspring, fertilisation type, nutrition source, parental care)

quiz.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a hormone with its role in pregnancy, birth or lactation?
choices: Oxytocin: stops the uterine lining from forming
Prolactin: supports milk production after birth
Progesterone: causes labour contractions
hCG: produced by the mother's breasts to make milk
quiz.rationale: Prolactin supports milk production. Oxytocin triggers contractions, progesterone maintains the uterine lining, and hCG signals the corpus luteum to remain active.
quiz.placement: Model: exit ticket (one hormone and its role) and revised class model

lessons.title: Helping Where Nature Needs a Hand: Debating IVF, Surrogacy and Sperm Banking

quiz.prompt: Many people believe that a baby born through IVF grows entirely in a test tube. Which statement about IVF is correct?
choices: Fertilisation happens in the fallopian tube, and only the sperm is prepared in the laboratory
Fertilisation and the whole development of the baby happen in a laboratory dish until birth
Fertilisation happens in a dish in the laboratory, and the embryo is then placed in the uterus where it develops until birth
Fertilisation happens in the uterus, and the baby is then moved to a laboratory incubator to grow
quiz.rationale: IVF replaces only fertilisation and the first few days of embryo growth outside the body. The embryo is transferred to the uterus, where implantation and pregnancy continue.
quiz.placement: Predict: Think-Pair-Share on where fertilisation happens in IVF and where the baby develops

quiz.prompt: A frog releases thousands of eggs into water, while a cow produces one calf after months inside her body. Which statement correctly describes how IVF fertilisation compares with these natural methods?
choices: IVF fertilisation and development are both inside the body like in cows, so nothing is done in a laboratory
IVF fertilisation is outside the body like in frogs, but the embryo then develops inside the uterus like in cows
IVF fertilisation and development are both outside the body like in frogs
IVF fertilisation is inside the body like in cows, and the embryo then develops in water like in frogs
quiz.rationale: In IVF, eggs and sperm meet in a dish (similar to external fertilisation in frogs), but the embryo is transferred to the uterus to develop, as in internal development in cows and humans.
quiz.placement: Explain: comparing IVF with external fertilisation in frogs and internal fertilisation in cows

quiz.prompt: A woman in Nakuru has blocked fallopian tubes, so her eggs cannot meet sperm. Which technology best addresses her problem?
choices: Taking FSH injections only, so that the tubes open
Sperm banking, where sperm is frozen and stored
Surrogacy only, because her uterus cannot work
IVF, where fertilisation takes place in a dish outside the body
quiz.rationale: IVF bypasses the blocked tubes by fertilising eggs in a dish and then placing the embryo in the uterus. Her uterus is normal, so surrogacy is not needed, and sperm banking does not solve a blocked tube.
quiz.placement: Observe: Case study A (Nakuru, blocked fallopian tubes) in the evidence table

quiz.prompt: A young man in Nairobi is about to start cancer treatment that may damage his testes. He wants to be able to have children later. Which option is the most suitable?
choices: Surrogacy, because a woman carries his sperm
Using IVF now, because it makes sperm inside the testes
Sperm banking, by freezing and storing his sperm before treatment
Hormone injections of FSH after the treatment is complete
quiz.rationale: Sperm banks freeze and store sperm so it can be used later, for example in IVF, even if the testes are damaged by treatment. IVF does not make sperm and surrogacy is about carrying a pregnancy.
quiz.placement: Observe: Case study D (Nairobi, cancer treatment and sperm bank)

quiz.prompt: A woman in Mombasa was born without a functional uterus but has healthy ovaries. Which technology allows her to have a genetically related child?
choices: FSH injections, which build a new uterus
Surrogacy, where another woman carries the embryo in her uterus
Sperm banking, where sperm is frozen
Natural fertilisation in the fallopian tubes followed by development in the ovary
quiz.rationale: Without a working uterus, the embryo cannot develop in her body. In surrogacy, an embryo (usually made by IVF) is carried by another woman. Hormones cannot create a uterus.
quiz.placement: Observe: Case study E (Mombasa, absent uterus, surrogacy)

quiz.prompt: A woman in Eldoret has irregular ovulation because her body makes too little FSH and LH. In the IVF flowchart, what is the role of FSH injections?
choices: They freeze the sperm for storage
They stimulate several eggs to mature in the ovaries so the eggs can be collected
They make the embryo implant without a uterus
They carry the embryo into the uterus
quiz.rationale: FSH stimulates the ovaries to mature several eggs. These eggs are then collected for fertilisation in a dish.
quiz.placement: Explain: hormonal flowchart of IVF (hormone injections stimulate eggs to mature)

quiz.prompt: Which list shows the correct order of the main steps of IVF?
choices: Egg collection, implantation, fertilisation in a dish, hormone stimulation, embryo transfer to the uterus
Embryo transfer to the uterus, egg collection, fertilisation in a dish, hormone stimulation, implantation
Hormone stimulation of eggs, egg collection, fertilisation in a dish, embryo transfer to the uterus, implantation
Fertilisation in a dish, hormone stimulation of eggs, implantation, egg collection, embryo transfer
quiz.rationale: Eggs must first be stimulated and collected, then fertilised in a dish. The early embryo is transferred to the uterus, where implantation follows.
quiz.placement: Explain: building the IVF concept map or hormonal flowchart in pairs

quiz.prompt: During the class debate, a learner says: "If a couple cannot have a child, it must be the woman's fault." Which response is scientifically correct?
choices: Infertility can be caused by problems in the man, the woman, or both, and male factors such as low sperm count account for many cases
Infertility in men never happens because sperm is made in large numbers
Infertility is caused only by cultural beliefs and not by body problems
Infertility is only caused by the woman, because only she carries the baby
quiz.rationale: The lesson corrects the myth that infertility is always the woman's problem. Male causes, such as low sperm count, account for a large share of cases.
quiz.placement: End: debate and explain-phase discussion correcting myths about infertility

lessons.title: Shared Decisions, Hormonal Health and Biotechnology: Our Final Explanation of How Animals Reproduce

quiz.prompt: A frog near Kisumu lays thousands of eggs, but a cow gives birth to only one calf at a time. Which statement best explains this difference?
choices: Frog eggs have hard shells, so many of them are needed to break through
Frogs are smaller than cows, so their bodies are able to make more eggs than a cow can
Frogs fertilise eggs in water with no parental care, so many eggs are lost to predators and the environment, while a cow's young develop inside the body and are cared for
Cows produce hormones and frogs do not, so cows cannot make many young
quiz.rationale: External fertilisation with no parental care means high losses, so many eggs are needed. Internal development and care in cows protect the young, so one calf is enough.
quiz.placement: Predict: sticky-note prediction on why frogs lay thousands of eggs but a cow has one calf

quiz.prompt: The uterus of a mammal has a thick, muscular wall. Which function does this structure fit best?
choices: It holds and protects the developing embryo and contracts to push the baby out at birth
It carries sperm from the testes to the outside of the body
It produces eggs and releases them every month
It produces sperm cells for fertilisation

quiz.prompt: In a certain snake, the eggs are fertilised inside the female. The eggs stay and hatch inside her body, and the young are born alive. The young feed on egg yolk, not through a placenta. How is this snake classified?

quiz.prompt: In a human pregnancy, the placenta joins the mother's body to the developing baby. What happens across the placenta?

The mother's blood and the baby's blood mix completely and flow in one loop

Only milk passes from the mother to the baby
